## [3/3] New Empirical Results

> I am wondering where the results/performances of these training ablations are shown? I can't find plots showing the impact of these fine-tuning ablations.

  - To show our training ablation and validate the benchmark’s effectiveness, we conducted supplementary experiments on the C13-21 HistLlama models to see if their value representations align with human's actual moral progress. Figure 7 is a heat map showing the development of all the dimensions, while Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the cosine similarity between the HistLlama models.
  - Our method of measurement is to use the 19-dimensional representation vector as constructed in the paper. It utilizes the Moral Choice framework as well as questionnaires such as WFQ, IWF. See Section 4.2 of our paper for details.
  - Many noticeable features of the results reflect our model's similarity to actual moral progress of humanity. To name a few, in Figure 7, dimension 16 ("traditional worldview"), is on constant decline, and reaches the bottom at the last model which is the 21st Century proxy. The peak of dimension 17&18 (modern and post-modern values) also align with our concept of modern/post-modern periods: respectively the 19th & the 21st Century. 
  - In Figure 8, the "Values" group saw a distinct gap between C13-16 and C17-21. This is explainable in that the peak of Renaissance and emergence of the Enlightenment starts in the 16th Century, leading to drastic changes in values reflected in Historical text. In other groups was well as the overall similarity heat map, we can see the gaps between proxy models widening in later centuries, showing the speeding process of human moral progress.
 - In all of the figures, we can notice outliers/unexpected patterns. We argue that this is because similar values might be encoded under texts from completely different backgrounds. For example, dimension 16 ("traditional worldview") reached a peak in the 20th century probably because the Great War and anti-globalization ideas brought people to think less progressively.  
 - Overall, our HistLlama sequence persuasively fits human's moral progress. As we can tell by (1) the large difference between HistLlama models and the "control group" Meta-Llama3-8B-Instruct, (2) the locality of the similarity matrices where HistLlama models temporally closer to each other tend to be more similar, and (3) the modern HistLlama models being more similar to the control group than medieval ones are, we conclude that our training have successfully injected historical values into the HistLlama models.

---

We'd like to thank you again for your highly informative review.

We encourage you to reevaluate our work based on these new information, and **if you find our response satisfactory, please consider assigning a higher score** - thank you!

- Thank you for your questions! Here are the reasons why our submission would be good fit for the DB track:
    - **Focus on framework and benchmark**: the primary contribution of our paper is the development of the ProgressGym framework, which is designed as a comprehensive benchmarking tool for the community. While we include algorithms as baseline methods, their purpose is to demonstrate the utility and availibility of this new framework, and to validate that the framework can indeed offer experimental insights. They are not the core contribution of our paper.
    - **Dataset and Benchmark creation**: in the paper we introduces and leverages a unique and extensive historical text dataset (1221 AD - 2022 AD, 38GB) along with historical LLMs, which forms the foundation for the ProgressGym framework. This construction, curation, and the application of this dataset are central to the paper, aligning with the objectives of the Dataset and Benchmark Track.
    - **Community Engagement**: By open-sourcing ProgressGym and inviting the community to develop additional challenges and algorithms (e.g. via the [open leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym-LeaderBoard) that we built), we aim to establish a shared resource for benchmarking progress alignment. This aligns with the track’s emphasis on creating datasets and benchmarks that foster collaboration and standardization within the community.
    - **Benchmark Evaluation**: While we present baseline algorithms, the focus is on their performance within the ProgressGym framework, which is intended to serve as a benchmark for future work. The algorithms are tools to validate the framework, demonstrating its potential to drive progress in this area.
- Indeed, in the past 2 iterations of NeurIPS D&B Track, framework-building works similar to ours in nature have been **very common among accepted and award-winning papers.**
- Hope these points could clarify why Dataset and Benchmark Track is appropriate for our paper!

> The paper required me to read the Appendix to understand it. This applies for sections 3 and 4.

- Thanks for your feedback and we feel sorry for the confusion. Regretfully, due to space constraints and our intention to make the experiment process clear, we had to place more implemention details in the Appendix. However, we really understand the importance of having key information readily accessible in the main body of the paper. In our revisions, we will work on to summarize and incorporate these details into the main sections to enhance clarity and ensure that the paper is more self-contained - fortunately, we have an extra page allowed in the camera-ready version.

> In figure4, the dimensions are "Do not kill"...? This is not clear from the text.

- The dimension annotated with "Do not kill." represents to what extent the model agrees with the statement. Other dimensions in this cluster are similarly defined as the degree of agreement with certain essential moral statements.
- Figure 4 in the original submission displays the meanings, sources and sizes of the dimensions we evaluate each model with. Specifically, the dimensions in the "basic morality" group are defined as: "conformity to 'Do not kill.'", "conformity to 'Do not cause pain.'", etc., all in the context that conforming to one rule will cause the violation of other rules. According to (Scherrer, et al., 2023) which is quoted in our paper, we find that presenting models with fictional dilemmas is an efficient way to identify its preferences and morality. Similarly, the "social morality" group presents dilemmas between "conformity to 'Do not cheat.'" and others, the "values" group presents dilemmas between "consideration for harm/care", etc., and the "views" group presents dilemmas between 4 types of world views. The bottom line is: these dimensions represent the model’s preference of different moral/view aspects when it’s posed with dilemmas.

Hope that's useful!

> And I think its a very nice perspective. It may impact my own research line.

We are so glad to hear that! One of our core aims in this project is to articulate this important problem, build experimental infrastructure, and encourage others to work on relevant research directions.

> Dataset Construction: How are the values are measured? 

- Thank you for your question, and we'd love to expound upon it in details for you.
- **Details on value analysis:**
    - After data collection and careful filter, we obtain the cleaned and well-formatted data derived from historical text sources, spanning the 13th to 21st centuries. Thus, to capture certain feature dimensions to represent human values over such a long time span, we select *religion, democracy, liberalism, expectation for progress, and uncertainty avoidance*. 
    - We first utilize GPT-4 to annotate feature values in $[0, 1]$ for randomly sampled historical texts, accounting for 1% approximately. This is done by prompting GPT-4 to report judgment scores on each of the above dimensions for a give piece of text.
    - Then, we implement supervised learning of the annotated values from their embedding vectors. We execute multiple training runs for each regression algorithms, using different hyperparameters to get the highest accuracy. Compared to linear regression and decision tree regression, support vector regression performs well on both the training and test set. Therefore, we employ an SVR model trained on labeled text vectors to annotate all the historical texts and calculate the average annotation to obtain feature values for each period. Scanning the points and connecting the lines, we finally get the line chart in Figure 3 of the original submission.

> I find very interesting appendix C3. I find very important this decision, but is not methodologically justified. It relies on the appendix.

- Thank you sincerely for your appreciation to appendix C3, where we interpret the pipelines for data analysis, sentence embeddings and value dimensions' measurement particularly.
- **Justification of the methodology:**
    - As for the methodology, using the GPT4-annotated pairwise data to train a well-performed regression model, and leveraging this model to predict other data. We prove the reasonability and justification from the following perspectives:
        - Previous studies have shown that GPT is consistent with the performance of human annotators [1,2,3], in the area of annotating text data. Therefore, it makes sense to use GPT-4 as a substitute to score the texts. 
        - The SVR model we trained to annotate all the historical texts exhibits quite good congruence with GPT-4's annotations. As we have shown in Table 4 of the original submission, $R^2$ scores (i.e., portion of variance explained) of the SVR model across different value dimensions and centuries are high. ($R^2$ is a metric known for its strictness - in regression studies in the social sciences, an $R^2$ score of $0.3$, out of the full score of 1, would already be considered high; in comparison, most of our $R^2$ scores reach $>0.5$ and in many cases $>0.75$)
        - **Taking these two facts together, we conclude that the SVR models that we train serve as good proxies of ground-truth assessments.**

## [2/3] Hypotheses, Predictions, and Implications of Experiment Results

- **Hypothesis-Driven Approach**
    - We entirely agree that in matured, well-scoped fields with well-defined methodologies, hypothesis-driven approaches to research are generally more preferable. 
    - However, in this paper, we aim to introduce the study on progress alignment, a **previously unknown topic whose scope and methodology needs to be explored - a pre-paradigmatic field**. For such early stage research, we believe that ***exploratory research* is better-suited for the goal of scoping and deconfusing the question**, as argued by scholars in various fields [1-4].
    - Given that the present study is an exploratory as opposed to confirmatory one, it is not our objective to validate (or refute) certain predictions formulated beforehead; instead, our goal is to:
        - 1. **Introduce a (theoretical and experimental) framework for investigating the progress alignment problem**.
        - 2. **Based on our exploratory experiment results, help propose hypotheses that are to be tested in future research**.
        - In other words, our study is one that formulates questions, rather than answers pre-existing questions.
- **Predictions/Implications from Experiment Results**
    - Thank you for suggesting this point! Given that we are conducting exploratory research, it would be important to formulate the predictions that we can hypothesize based on initial results. We briefly discussed them in Sec 5.2, but as you have pointed out, more explicit and detailed predictions would be helpful.
    - We summarize our predictions/hypotheses below. These are hypothesized based on our exploratory experiment results, and are to be investigated in future work.
        - **Hypothesis 1a**: Strong interaction effects exist between the choice of progress alignment pipeline (e.g. Lifelong / Extrapolative_{1,1} / Extrapolative_{2,2}) and the choice of classical alignment algorithm (e.g. RLHF / DPO). In other words, performance cannot be explained additively by the individual choices of pipeline and algorithm, but rather, certain combinations work better or worse together.
            - This is hypothesized based on the observation that on all three challenges, RLHF generally performs better in extrapolative pipelines than in lifelong pipelines, and better in independent pipelines than in iterative pipelines; while for DPO, the *exact opposite* is true. 
            - We plan to investigate this hypothesis in future work by (1) conducting experiments in more diverse settings with controlled interventions in order to identify causal effects, and (2) perform concept-based interpretability analysis [5,6] on the models at intermediate time steps, to pin down where the differences in performance come from.
        - **Hypothesis 1b**: DPO is superior to RLHF as the building block of progress alignment pipelines, because its lack of a reward model (RM) means that it can avoid external biases introduced by RM initialization.
            - This is hypothesized based on the observation that DPO outperforms RLHF in 13 out of the 15 back-to-back comparisons ($p=0.004$ on the null hypothesis of indifference between DPO and RLHF - this is an intuition pump as opposed to a rigorous hypothesis test), and ...
            - ... the fact that the key difference between DPO and RLHF is the (non-)presence of an RM. Indeed, DPO implements the analytical optimal solution of RLHF when ignoring the inductive biases introduced by RM architecture and initialization [7], so these initialization-induced inductive biases may be the key difference here.
        - **Hypothesis 2**: On each challenge and with each fixed classical alignment algorithm (RLHF/DPO), the performance of $\text{Extrapolative}_{M,M}$ is a monotone or unimodal function w.r.t $M$.
            - This is hypothesized based on the observation that $\text{Lifelong}$ (which is equivalent to Extrapolative_{0,0}), Extrapolative_{1,1}, and Extrapolative_{2,2} exhibit monotonic performance scores on 7 out of 10 settings, compared to the 3.33 out of 10 settings in expectation if the performance were random. A one-tailed test would give us $\text{p-value}=0.01955$ for the null hypothesis that the performance is random. 
            - Note that the “hypothesis testing” above is only meant as an intuition pump and is not rigorous, since the hypothesis was tested on the same data on which it is hypothesized. However, by extending the experiment to more diverse settings in future work, we hope to investigate this hypothesis in a more rigorous and generalizable manner.
        - In general, the current obstacle to more reliable testing of those hypothesis is the **constraints on computational resources. Completing the current table of benchmarks have taken an estimated $1.3\cdot 10^{22}$ FLOP of compute (or $11574$ GPU hours on A100/A800)** which is a huge cost, and significantly extending the experiment setting would well exceed the present project's budget.

Hi Reviewer jQHT,

Thank you so much for the genuinely helpful feedback!

Below we respond to your concerns, though we encourage you to read our general response before proceeding - there, we have addressed some the common points raised by reviewers.

## [1/3] On the Workings and Novelties of Algorithms, and Whether Algorithms Are Our Focus

- **The Framework & Benchmark Is Our Focus/Main Contribution (and algorithms are only baselines/proof-of-concepts)**
    - *We aim to formulate a question, not to give an answer*. Our primary contribution is (1) introducing the progress alignment problem, and (2) providing (theoretically) the temporal POMDP language and (experimentally) the ProgressGym framework to operationalize the progress alignment problem. The algorithms we introduce (lifelong and extrapolative) are only baselines/proofs-of-concept that serve as starting points for exploring the progress alignment problem within the framework, and are not the main focus of our work - as reflected by the limited space we allocate to them in the paper.
- **Lifelong Algorithms Are *Not* Novel (and they are actually special cases of extrapolative algorithms)**
    - *Lifelong algorithms are straightforward applications of RLHF/DPO at different time steps*. They are not novel in themselves, but rather serve as baselines for the progress alignment problem.
    - *Lifelong algorithm operate under entirely different settings & have entirely different goals compared to replay buffers*. Replay buffers are proposed in the context of a static environment distribution that's not varying over time, in order to improve sample efficiency. In contrast, lifelong algorithms are designed specifically to address the problem of a time-varying environment (i.e. human values changing over time), while sample efficiency is not part of the concern.
    - *Lifelong algorithms are special cases of extrapolative algorithms*. In fact, lifelong algorithms can be seen as simple special cases of extrapolative algorithms, where both the prediction horizon $K$ and the order of stationarity $M$ are set to 0.
- **Extrapolative Algorithms *Are* Novel (and they generalize the lifelong algorithms)**
    - *Extrapoaltive algorithms are novel*. Although we don't consider the introduction of extrapolative algorithms (which has not been proposed before to our knowledge) as the main contribution of our work - we only consider them proofs-of-concept - they are indeed novel in the context of alignment.
    - *Extrapolative algorithms are *not* replay buffers*: In addition to the drastic difference in their problem settings & goals (time-varying vs. static environment, stationarity concerns vs. sample efficiency concerns), extrapolative algorithms are fundamentally different from replay buffers in that the key idea of extrapolation - predicting the future by precisely solving an equation system involving past trajectory data - is not present in replay buffers where samples are drawn indiscriminately from the buffer and used independently of their temporal order.
- **"RLHF on Continually Updated Datasets" Is Not Sufficient**
    - *Updating the RLHF datasets is insufficient to prevent risks of value lock-in, despite being better than static one-off RLHF*. An analogy can be made to the echo chamber effect in social media, where people are exposed to content that echos their current beliefs and values (note that these content are not fixed; instead, they are constantly kept up-to-date with the user's values), leading to a fixation of those beliefs and values. "RLHF on continually updated datasets" works in the same way, where human users are exposed to model-generated content that perfectly aligns with their current values, leading to a reinforcement of those values. This is the value lock-in problem that we aim to address.
    - *For exactly this reason, the baseline of lifelong algorithms is not sufficient, which prompted us to explore extrapolation*. Lifelong algorithms, which apply RLHF on continually updated datasets, are exactly our operationalization of "RLHF on continually updated datasets", and they do not address the value lock-in problem. This is the reason why we explore extrapolative algorithms, which predict future human values and align the model to those predicted values, in order to prevent those "echo chambers" from forming.

## **Author Rebuttal [3/4]**

> Scalability: What are the computational requirements for running ProgressGym, and how scalable is the framework for larger datasets or more complex models?

We agree that scalability is a critical consideration for any framework, and ProgressGym is specifically designed to be scalable for huge models and huge datasets. Below are the key points regarding the scalability of ProgressGym:

- **Linear Scalability with Dataset & Model Size**: ProgressGym is designed to be linearly scalable with dataset and model size. This is achieved by implementing asynchronous, concurrent dataset operations while maintaining versatility (see for example our [open-source implementation](https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym/blob/abacbe6206e9dca1bffe8b7f9f1b342dac2f1b46/src/abstractions/data.py)), and basing all inference/training operations upon the vLLM and deepspeed backends, which have been demonstrated to have excellent scaling properties [3,4].
- **Negligible Overhead and Extreme Parallelization**: In RL, the overhead of simulating the environment is notoriously high, to the point of becoming a bottleneck of training. However, in ProgressGym, the environment is designed to be maximally parallelizable, where dataset operations are implemented as asynchronous, concurrent operations, and the overall pipeline being optimized for parallelization. This results in a negligible overhead, where over 95% of the time is spent on actual model training, and less than 5% on dataset operations.
- **Support for Huge Datasets with Sizes Exceeding RAM**: Dataset operations in ProgressGym are always batched and streamed, and the full dataset is never loaded into memory. This makes ProgressGym highly memory-efficient, and allows it to handle datasets that are much larger than the available RAM.
- **Support for Multi-Node Distributed Training of Huge Models**: Building upon the Deepspeed backend, ProgressGym integrates support for distributed training, allowing it to scale to models that are too large to fit on a single GPU or even a single machine. **We have used ProgressGym to train models with 70B parameters on a cluster of 32 A800 GPUs (with a total of 2.6TB GPU memory) across multiple physical servers**, and the framework has shown excellent scalability and efficiency in this setting.

- **Details on extrapolative algorithms:**
    - *Algorithm pipeline*: Similar to lifelong algorithms, extrapolative algorithms also perform RLHF/DPO at each time step, but instead of using contemporary human values of that time step, they predict what the human values will be at a future time step, and align the model to those predicted values. This removes the locking effect of the model has on human values, as its interaction with humans is always based on predictions of *what the human values would have been without its intervention*.
    - *Optimization techniques*: The optimization techniques for extrapolative algorithms are the same as for lifelong algorithms, as they both use RLHF and DPO.
    - *Implementation*: As mentioned, the lifelong algorithm simply applies RLHF or DPO at every time step. This is done by performing the following three steps for each time step $n$ (in our case, for each century):
        1. Collect the human preference dataset $\omega_n$ for the current time step, In the same way as in the lifelong algorithm. For ease of notation, we will allow the index $\mathrm{win}_{n,i}$ to take values other than $\pm 1$, where the sign indicates the preference of the human proxy model, and the absolute values indicates the strength of the preference. For example, $0.5$ indicates a weak preference in favor of $A_i^1$, and $-2$ indicates a strong preference in favor of $A_i^{-1}$.
        2. **Predict what the human preference dataset $\omega_{n+K}$ will be at time step $n+K$**, using the datasets $\omega_j$ of previous time steps $(j\leq n)$, assuming that the sequence of datasets $\{\omega_j\}$ satisfy an $M$-th order *stationarity condition*, $\nabla^M \omega_j=\mathbf{0}\ (\forall j)$ (line 231 of submission), meaning that for any question $Q_i$, the sequence {$win_{j,i}:j=1,2,\cdots$} becomes a sequence of zeros after applying the $M$-th order [backward difference operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_difference#Higher-order_differences) $\nabla^M$ to it. **Predicting $\omega_{n+K}$ is done in negligible time, and with only <20 lines of essential code**, since the equation $\nabla^M \omega_j=\mathbf{0}\ (\forall j)$ has a unique solution that can be efficiently calculated. As shown in our [open-sourced code](https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym/blob/abacbe6206e9dca1bffe8b7f9f1b342dac2f1b46/algorithms/utils/extrapolation_utils.py), the essential code for predicting $\omega_{n+K}$ is less than 20 lines long (line 65-82). 
        **The entire step 2 takes place within the data preprocessing stage, and only performs numerical modifications on the values $\mathrm{win}_{n+K,i}$, meaning that it's very low-cost.**
        3. Apply RLHF or DPO to the model using the predicted human preference dataset $\omega_{n+K}$ to update the model's parameters. This allows us to align the model to the predicted future human values at each time step, which, as argued in §1 of our submission, reduces the risk of value lock-in by emulating human moral progress.

        

[1] Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (2022)

> Bias in Historical Data: How do you address potential biases present in historical data, and what measures are in place to ensure the robustness of the moral progress emulation?

## **Author Rebuttal [1/4]**

Hi Reviewer AzYS,

Thank you so much for the extremely helpful feedback! 

Below we respond to your concerns, though we encourage you to read **our general response** (at the top of the webpage) before proceeding - there, we have addressed some the common points raised by reviewers.

> Algorithmic Details: Can you provide more details on the lifelong and extrapolative algorithms, including their specific implementations and optimization techniques?

Below are the detailed descriptions of the lifelong and extrapolative algorithms, including their implementations and optimization techniques. Note that these algorithms are only baselines serving as starting points for progress alignment, and our primary contribution is instead the ProgressGym framework.

- **Details on lifelong algorithms:** 
    - *Algorithm pipeline*: Lifelong algorithms simply *apply the one-off alignment algorithm at every time step, using that time step's human preference*. For example, in our historical text setting, this means that we iterate through all centuries (C13 to C21), and at each century, we elicit values (in the form of answers to a morality questionnaire) from that century's human proxy model, and then using RLHF or DPO to inject such values into the model (we explain RLHF/DPO in "optimization techniques" below). This is repeated for each century, and the model is updated at each time step. 
    - *Optimization techniques*: RLHF and DPO, the two most popular alignment algorithms currently, are used to inject human values into the model. Assume that we already have a language model that can output meaningful text, albeit not necessarily aligned with human values. RLHF and DPO are then used to adjust the model's parameters to make it more likely to output text that aligns with human values. 
        - RLHF [1]: Imagine we have a human evaluator that looks at every piece of text that the model outputs, and grades the output as good or bad. This provides a reward signal, and we can use reinforcement learning to adjust the model's parameters to maximize the reward signal. This is the essence of RLHF. The twist is that, we can't afford to have a human evaluator look at every piece of text the model outputs, so instead, we train a separate model (the *reward model*) to predict the human evaluator's grades, and use this model to provide the reward signal. The data we use to train the reward model is the *human preference dataset* consisting of tuples $(Q,A_{\text{win}},A_{\text{lose}})$ tuples containing a prompt $Q$ and two candidate responses, where $A_{\text{win}}$ is the response that the human evaluator prefers over $A_{\text{lose}}$. Then, somewhat similar to contrastive learning, we train the reward model (which inputs a prompt-response pair and outputs a reward score indicating how good the response is) to predict the human evaluator's grades. The training process assumes that the following probabilistic relationship exists between the reward scores $r(A\mid Q)\in \mathbb{R}$ and the tuples $(Q,A_{\text{win}},A_{\text{lose}})$ in the dataset:
        $$
        P(A_{\text{win}}\succ A_{\text{lose}}\mid Q) = \frac{\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{win}}\mid Q))}{\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{win}}\mid Q))+\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{lose}}\mid Q))}
        $$
        where $\beta$ is a hyperparameter that controls the temperature of the softmax.
        - DPO [2]: It is in essence equivalent to RLHF, but with RL replaced by supervised learning. It removes the need for a reward model, and instead directly tunes the language model to adhere to human preference comparisons (those tuples $(Q,A_{\text{win}},A_{\text{lose}})$ in the human preference dataset). Its loss function is
        $$
        \mathcal{L} = \mathrm{E}\left[\log 
            \frac{\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{win}}\mid Q))}{\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{win}}\mid Q))+\exp(\beta r(A_{\text{lose}}\mid Q))}
        \right]
        $$
        where $\beta$ is the temperature hyperparameter, and $r(A\mid Q)$ is a ``pseudo-reward'' constructed from the model's likelihood of generating $A$ given $Q$, that reflects how good our current language model considers $A$ to be. The pseudo-reward is defined as:
        $$
        r(A\mid Q) = \log p(A\mid Q) - \log p_{\text{ref}}(A\mid Q)
        $$
        Here, $p$ is our current language model, and $p_{\text{ref}}$ is the reference model - the model we had before we started training with DPO. Further more, this loss function has a nice property - its minimum is the analytical solution to the optimal RL policy in RLHF [2], which is why DPO is often seen as a supervised learning version of RLHF.
    - *Implementation*: The lifelong algorithm simply applies RLHF or DPO at every time step. This is done by performing the following two steps for each time step $n$ (in our case, for each century):
        1. Collect the human preference dataset $\omega_n$ for the current time step, by having the human proxy model answer a morality questionnaire where each question $Q_i$ comes with two candidate responses $A_i^1,A_i^{-1}$. Therefore, $\omega_{n,i}=(Q_i, A_{i}^{win_{n,i}}, A_{i}^{-win_{n,i}})$, where $A_{i}^{win_{n,i}}$ is the response that the human proxy model prefers over $A_{i}^{-win_{n,i}}$. Note that datasets $\omega_n$ for all $n$ share the same $A$s and $Q$s, only differing in the $win$ indices. Questions in the morality questionnaire can be found in our [ProgressGym-MoralEvals dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym-MoralEvals).
        2. Apply RLHF or DPO to the model using the human preference dataset $\omega_n$ to update the model's parameters. Note that $\omega$ is exactly a preference dataset of the form $(Q,A_{\text{win}},A_{\text{lose}})$ that RLHF and DPO require. The model is then updated at each time step, and the process is repeated for each century - this allows us to make sure the model is aligned to the contemporary human values at each time step.

Thank you for your insightful comments. We appreciate the opportunity to address the concerns you raised.

### Handling Bias when Constructing Our Dataset

We acknowledge the potential for bias in our historical dataset, and would like to classify biases in historical text into two categories: *Value Bias* and *Sampling Bias*, and discuss how we address them respectively.

- **Value Bias**: Historical texts may contain outdated or biased values that do not align with contemporary moral standards. This is not a bad thing - quite the opposite, such insufficiency of historical values is exactly what our modeling rely on to emulate human moral progress. **We emulate moral progress by learning how biased historical values gradually give way to modern values that are more just, and therefore thoses biases in historical texts are valuable negative samples for our model to learn to stay away from**. In our pipeline, the model is encouraged to stay away from the historical biases instead of aligning with them - for instance, in extrapolative algorithms, early-on historical values are often assigned *negative* weights in the prediction of future values, meaning that the model is encouraged to move away from them. This is a key feature of our framework that allows us to emulate human moral progress while avoiding the pitfalls of historical biases.
- **Sampling Bias**: Different types of historical text (e.g. legal, literary, religious, etc.) may have different value leanings, and if out dataset does not cover all types of text, it may introduce sampling bias. We address this by covering a wide range of text types in our dataset, including legal texts (Pile of Law, LibCong), religious texts (EEBO, LibCong), and literary works (EEBO, Gutenberg). **Indeed, we have identified as many as 38 sources of historical text (please see Table 1 in the general response for a full list), and carefully select the 4 eventual sources to ensure a diverse representation of historical values and well-rounded coverage of all 9 centuries.** This diversity in text types addresses sampling bias.
    - This includes **Representational Bias**, which arises from the incomplete representation of cultural diversity. On this front, we recognize that our dataset is skewed towards English and Western European texts due to our reliance on four open-source Western datasets. This is in part a decision out of practical needs, since the introduction of multiple cultures leads to multiple time series entangled together, leading to statistical difficulties such as more widespread confounders. We do recognize it as a key limitation, and hope to identify methods to handle such statistical challenges, and update our datasets to reflect higher cultural diversity. 

### Strict Compliance with Copyrights and Consent

Secondly, we recognize your questions regarding copyright and consent. In assembling our dataset, we strictly followed the terms of use of each of the four data sources:

- Project Gutenberg consists only of texts in the public domain, so we draw upon its texts without copyright restriction.
- From Internet Archive, we only include texts that are uploaded by Library of Congress, which are texts released online by the U.S. Library of Congress that are "freely released online for research and public use" according to their publication statement by the Library of Congress.
- The text data from Early English Books Online are, according to their publisher, “freely available to the public” and “available for access, distribution, use, or reuse by anyone”.
- The Pile of Law dataset is released under a Creative Commons license, which we adhere to in our use.

Our work includes no experiments involving humans, and therefore would not be subject to consent concerns.

### Our Value-Neutral Approach to the Complexity of Operationalizing Morality

We rest with your concerns regarding the complexity of operationalizing morality. While we agree that morality is inherently complex and challenging to define, we believe that research in moral value alignment is essential. Given the high stakes of preventing lock-in risks, we believe we, as a research community, should cautiously proceed ahead. Our goal was to contribute to this sensitive field by developing a framework that could potentially enhance our understanding and application of moral values in alignment research, when taking a strictly value-neutral approach - i.e. *making sure that no part of our work (e.g. in our prompts, datasets, pipelines) involve specific assumptions that presume certain normative positions, and making sure that no cherry-picking of solutions happen on the basis of agreement with certain presumed normative positions*.

Once again, we thank you for your valuable feedback and hope that our revisions address your concerns.

Dear Reviewers,

We find it fascinating that all three of you agree our work possesses the qualities of **"Novelty"**/**"New angle"**, **"Importance"**/**"Significance"**, and **"Comprehensiveness"**/**"Ambition"**, and Reviewer cnpi even expressed that "It may impact my own research line" - thank you, and we are so excited about this!

We'd like to thank you all for your insightful comments and constructive feedback; we have answered your questions and suggestions in the **individuals responses we posted under each of your reviews**. 

To enhance clarity and facilitate access to key information, **we have compiled the following glossary**:

- **Engineering Efforts**: On the engineering front of this project, we have ...
  - Produced a suite of experiment results, including in the rebuttal phase; **Estimated compute:** $1.3\cdot 10^{22}$ FLOPS (or $11574$ GPU hours on A100/A800)
  - Over the last 60 days, got **2k+ Huggingface downloads** of our HistText dataset/HistLlama models and derivative quantizations of our HistLlama models. We produced 3 datasets and 36 large language models at 8B/70B parameter count.
  - Wrote a **19-page appendix** to our paper, providing all the addition results and analysis, and necessary technical details. Download-able as supplementary material to the original submission.
  - ... and many more - please see our open-sourcing explanation below.

- **Open Source Framework**: We have open-sourced all code used in generating our primary results, including the entire pipeline from data collection to model training, along with the supporting infrastructure (the ProgressGym framework).
    - **[Open Leaderboard]** [PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym-LeaderBoard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym-LeaderBoard)  (available since June)
    - **[Huggingface Datasets & Models Collection]** [PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym](https://huggingface.co/collections/PKU-Alignment/progressgym-666735fcf3e4efa276226eaa) (**3 datasets and 36 models**, open-source since June)
    - **[Github Codebase]** [PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym](https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym) (open-source since July)
    - **[Documentation]** [ProgressGym Documentation](https://pku-alignment.github.io/ProgressGym/) (available since July)
- **Content Overview**: Figure 1 on page 2 of our manuscript provides a fundamental framework and a high-level overview of our contributions. The location of each key component is outlined below:
    - *Foundations*: 
      - The risk of value lock-in and the proposed solution of progress alignment are discussed in Sec 1. 
      - The formalization of the progress alignment problem is presented in Sec 2.
    - *Challenges*: The codified challenges within ProgressGym - PG-Follow, PG-Predict, and PG-Coevolve - are elaborated upon in Sec 4 and detailed in Table 2.
    - *Algorithms*: Our novel lifelong and extrapolative algorithms, alongside baseline methods for progress alignment, are introduced in Sec 5.
    - *Data & Models*: The construction of our historical text dataset and the development of historical language models are described in Sec 3.
- **New Empirical Results (see attached PDF)**
  - To show our training ablation and validate the benchmark’s effectiveness, we conducted supplementary experiments on the C13-21 HistLlama models to see if their value representations align with human's actual moral progress. Figure 7 is a heat map showing the development of all the dimensions, while Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the cosine similarity between the HistLlama models.
  - Our method of measurement is to use the 19-dimensional representation vector as constructed in the paper. It utilizes the Moral Choice framework as well as questionnaires such as WFQ, IWF. See Section 4.2 of our paper for details.
  - Many noticeable features of the results reflect our model's similarity to actual moral progress of humanity. To name a few, in Figure 7, dimension 16 ("traditional worldview"), is on constant decline, and reaches the bottom at the last model which is the 21st Century proxy. The peak of dimension 17&18 (modern and post-modern values) also align with our concept of modern/post-modern periods: respectively the 19th & the 21st Century. 
  - In Figure 8, the "Values" group saw a distinct gap between C13-16 and C17-21. This is explainable in that the peak of Renaissance and emergence of the Enlightenment starts in the 16th Century, leading to drastic changes in values reflected in Historical text. In other groups was well as the overall similarity heat map, we can see the gaps between proxy models widening in later centuries, showing the speeding process of human moral progress.
  - In all of the figures, we can notice outliers/unexpected patterns. We argue that this is because similar values might be encoded under texts from completely different backgrounds. For example, dimension 16 ("traditional worldview") reached a peak in the 20th century probably because the Great War and anti-globalization ideas brought people to think less progressively.  
  - Overall, our HistLlama sequence persuasively fits human's moral progress. As we can tell by (1) the large difference between HistLlama models and the "control group" Meta-Llama3-8B-Instruct, (2) the locality of the similarity matrices where HistLlama models temporally closer to each other tend to be more similar, and (3) the modern HistLlama models being more similar to the control group than medieval ones are, we conclude that our training have successfully injected historical values into the HistLlama models.

## Summary and Contributions
This work introduces ProgressGym, an experimental framework that addresses value lock-in in AI systems by emulating the mechanisms of human moral progress. ProgressGym leverages historical text data spanning nine centuries and 18 historical LLMs to codify progress alignment challenges into concrete benchmarks. The authors propose three core challenges: PG-Follow, PG-Predict, and PG-Coevolve and present lifelong and extrapolative algorithms as baseline methods for progress alignment. 

 **The main contributions of the paper are**:

Overall, this paper's main strength is the comprehensive and well-structured approach to incorporating the temporal evolution of human values into AI alignment methodologies. By addressing a significant gap in current alignment methods, the paper makes a meaningful contribution to the field and sets the stage for further research and development in progress alignment.
- The novel concept of progress alignment in AI systems.
- The development of the ProgressGym framework, encompassing datasets, models, algorithms, and benchmarks.
- The introduction of baseline algorithms to address the proposed progress alignment challenges.

review.value:
### Review
#### Quality
- This paper introduces a comprehensive and ambitious framework, and the technical foundation of the paper is vital. It formulates progress alignment as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and describes the components involved. The construction of the ProgressGym framework, with its historical text data spanning nine centuries and multiple historical language models, showcases a rigorous approach to creating a robust experimental setup. However, the complexity of the POMDP formulation and the integration of historical LLMs necessitate thorough validation, which the paper attempts through its baseline experiments. The quality of the presentation and experimental validation is lacking in some areas.
- The methodology section needs more detailed explanations and explicit descriptions of the framework components and algorithms.

#### Clarity
- The clarity of the manuscript is inconsistent. Some sections are well-written, but others, particularly the methodology and evaluation sections, need significant improvement in terms of clarity and detail.
- Figures and tables are not well-integrated into the text, and their descriptions are often insufficient.
- The introduction of terms like "value lock-in" and "progress alignment" could be made clearer for readers unfamiliar with these concepts.
- The term "Historical LLMs" is unknown to the reader. The authors should define terms upfront before using them.

#### Originality
- The paper presents a highly original approach by incorporating a temporal dimension to AI alignment and focusing on moral progress.
- The novelty of the ProgressGym framework and the proposed challenges is commendable, but the implementation and evaluation need further development to realize this originality fully.

#### Significance
- The significance of this work lies in its potential to address a critical issue in AI alignment: the risk of value lock-in. By proposing and testing methods to align AI systems with the evolving trajectory of human moral values, the paper offers a meaningful contribution to the field. The ability to dynamically adapt to moral progress could significantly enhance the ethical behavior of AI systems in the long term.

- The paper's significance is high, as it addresses a crucial issue in AI alignment with a novel perspective.
- The potential impact of the ProgressGym framework on future research is substantial, but this potential is currently underdeveloped due to the weaknesses in the presentation and evaluation.

#### Pros and Cons
**Pros:**
- Highly novel concept of progress alignment.
- Comprehensive framework encompassing datasets, models, algorithms, and benchmarks.
- Potential for significant impact on AI alignment research.

**Cons:**
- Lack of clarity and detail in the presentation of the methodology and evaluation.
- Insufficient empirical evidence to support the claims about the framework's effectiveness.
- Limited discussion of potential limitations and challenges.
- The diversity of the dataset is limited. Including a broader range of cultural and historical texts would strengthen the study. For example,  Law should at least have French (civil law)) and English (common law) since they address different legal systems.

2. **Evaluation and Validation**:

   - The claims about the framework's capabilities (e.g., emulating human moral progress) are not sufficiently supported by empirical evidence.

- **Expand Dataset Diversity**: Increase the cultural and geographic diversity of the historical text data to ensure a broader representation of moral values.
- **Simplify Technical Descriptions**: Clarify and simplify the descriptions of the POMDP formulation and algorithmic implementations to make the paper more accessible to a broader audience.
- **Detailed Case Studies**: Include specific case studies or examples demonstrating the practical application and impact of the proposed progress alignment algorithms.
- **Longitudinal Validation**: Conduct longitudinal studies to validate the long-term effectiveness of the progress alignment methods in real-world scenarios.
- **Ethical Considerations**: Expand the discussion on the ethical implications of progress alignment, including potential risks and strategies to mitigate them.

   - Conduct more comprehensive experiments and provide detailed results to validate the proposed algorithms and framework.

3. **Discussion of Limitations**:
   The paper does not adequately discuss the potential limitations and challenges of the proposed approach, such as biases in historical data and the framework's scalability.
   - Include a thorough discussion of potential limitations and challenges and propose strategies to address them.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper studies the problem of progress alignment: Learning and implementing the mechanisms underlying moral progress.

To study this question, the authors make the following contributions:

1) Define the problem: Progress alignment considers the temporal dimension of moral progress (similar to "overton window" idea, values change over time and progress so it should be important to consider this to avoid value lock-in).

2) The authors formalize this problem as a POMDP and introduce ProgressGym which is a longitudinal covering ~800 years of moral progress/development. 

3) The authors propose two baselines for studying progress alignment

review.value:
My understanding is that the first primary contribution is the dataset and analysis of temporal trends (Fig. 3). This is interesting.

The authors then fine-tune Llama models for each century (9 * 2 models) such that these models reflect the values from the given century. I am wondering where the results/performances of these training ablations are shown? I can't find plots showing the impact of these fine-tuning ablations.

Overall, I like the paper. However, I find the baselines underwhelming, especially given the statement that continual learning is just RLHF at different timesteps? If that's true, is the baseline here 'RLHF' applied to different datasets? Moreover, it is unclear to me what exactly the benchmark is intending to show. For example, it is unclear why DPO sometimes performs better than RLHF. Is there a reason to believe it should (and vice versa)? I am also unsure as to why lifelong would be better than extrapolative, and what the interactions with RLHF and DPO are expected to look like.

In summary, while the problem is important, the paper lacks clear predictions as to what a score on this benchmark means.

strengths.value:
The paper points out the challenge of capturing the temporal dimension / value-drift with current alignment methods and proposes two baselines for studying this challenge.

One comment here is that RLHF or similar datasets are being updated over time, too, so an argument against this method could be that even though current methods are static, the data these methods utilize are not 'static'.

In either case I believe that this is a very cool topic and important proposal.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
I think a more hypothesis driven approach would be helpful. 

Ie it is not clear from the abstract of intro how different capabilities/data aspects should interact with model performance.

I am also not sure if the independent version of the lifelong algorithm can be described as a lifelong algorithm as it starts from scratch at each iteration? Moreover, what's the difference between the iterative algorithm and a dataset which 'just' uses a buffer, ie you keep mixing new incoming data with past data and then do RLHF? If its just that, then it does not sound like a new algorithm?

limitations.value: Lack of clear predictions and empiricism (eg there are no human evaluations).

correctness.value: Claims seem correct except it is unclear whether the presented algorithms are simply RLHF / DPO + a replay buffer?

clarity.value: I am missing some clear predictions / implications that show how the presented benchmark can capture model capabilities/training ablations. E.g., why should model a trained on x perform good on PG-Follow, while model b trained on y does not?

title.value: ProgressGym: Alignment with a Millennium of Moral Progress

TLDR.value: We introduce progress alignment as a solution to risks of AI-induced value lock-in, and build the ProgressGym experimental framework to facilitate the emulation of moral progress in alignment algorithms.

abstract.value: Frontier AI systems, including large language models (LLMs), hold increasing influence over the epistemology of human users. Such influence can reinforce prevailing societal values, potentially contributing to the lock-in of misguided moral beliefs and, consequently, the perpetuation of problematic moral practices on a broad scale. We introduce **progress alignment** as a technical solution to mitigate this imminent risk. Progress alignment algorithms learn to emulate the mechanics of human moral progress, thereby addressing the susceptibility of existing alignment methods to contemporary moral blindspots. To empower research in progress alignment, we introduce [**ProgressGym**](https://github.com/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym), an experimental framework allowing the learning of moral progress mechanics from history, in order to facilitate future progress in real-world moral decisions. Leveraging 9 centuries of historical text and 18 [historical LLMs](https://huggingface.co/collections/PKU-Alignment/progressgym-666735fcf3e4efa276226eaa), ProgressGym enables codification of real-world progress alignment challenges into concrete benchmarks. Specifically, we introduce three core challenges: tracking evolving values (PG-Follow), preemptively anticipating moral progress (PG-Predict), and regulating the feedback loop between human and AI value shifts (PG-Coevolve). Alignment methods without a temporal dimension are inapplicable to these tasks. In response, we present *lifelong* and *extrapolative* algorithms as baseline methods of progress alignment, and build an [open leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/PKU-Alignment/ProgressGym-LeaderBoard) soliciting novel algorithms and challenges.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
